newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Crisis, scandal, riots mar Netanyahu's first year.
newsitem.headline: Crisis, scandal, riots mar Netanyahu's first year.

text.p: His peace talks with Palestinians are mired in crisis.
He nearly got indicted for corruption.
A year after right-winger Benjamin Netanyahu's election as prime minister, it is not clear where he is leading Israel.
Last May 29 "Bibi" -- as he is known -- ousted Nobel laureate Shimon Peres by fewer than 30,000 votes on a promise to guard Israeli security in the aftermath of suicide bombings.
Now, after a year marked by unprecedented West Bank and Gaza gunfights in September and a deadlock in the talks, the country is still split down the middle.
Opinion polls show half of Israel believes Netanyahu has failed even on the security front. Critics blame him for a peace stalemate they fear will slide into violence.
Backers see him as acting firmly and fearlessly in the face of Arab demands while pursuing a secure peace.

"In the last year when everyone said the peace process had collapsed and there was no peace and no process, we have had to take into account there was almost no terrorism...which is a big achievement," Communications Minister Limor Livnat told Reuters.
As for peacemaking, "All the predictions that everything is collapsing are not true," she said, citing an Israeli-Egyptian summit on Tuesday that she said ended in an atmosphere of hope.
In interviews Netanyahu points with pride at having handed over most of the West Bank town of Hebron, freed Palestinian women prisoners and eased a closure on Arab territories.

The 70 percent majority his Hebron deal got in parliament, backed by all but the far right, would have been the envy of late Labour Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, whose Oslo peace deals with the PLO garnered paper-thin majorities.
But to the dismay of Palestinians and his U.S. ally, Netanyahu also boasts of policies that have derailed peace.

He pledges allegiance to the Oslo accords he reluctantly inherited from Rabin and Peres. But he constantly reiterates he dislikes the deals, hampering U.S. efforts to foster trust between him and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Arafat, asked to describe his biggest problem with Netanyahu, told Israel's newspaper Haaretz this week: "He officially declared he opposes the Oslo agreement."
Palestinians accused Netanyahu of trying to pre-empt future peace talks when in March he broke ground for a Jewish settlement on Jerusalem land claimed by both sides.
They could not take him seriously when his government's decision on a troop redeployment gave them control over only a third of the West Bank land they had expected.
In such a climate, Palestinians are sceptical of Netanyahu's offer to close a deal in six months on the toughest issues yet.

His judgment will likely also come into question in the year ahead, as it did in the corruption scandal over a political appointment and in his opening of a tourist tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem which ignited violence last September.
Opinion polls, businessmen and Israelis left and right, all give Netanyahu low marks for management and integrity.

"Many times there was an impression conveyed that the government wasn't under adult supervision," Mark Heller, senior research associate at Tel Aviv University's Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies, told Reuters.
"I don't think that next year is going to be any better than the first," added Israeli political philosopher Meron Benvenisti. "I don't see any learning curve."

Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, has seized on his adversity to rally supporters, striking a resonant chord by lashing out at the media, the legal establishment and other parts of society he portrays as elites out to get him.

The technique may shore up support but it won't win him points for statesmanship. Instead it has fanned the flames of division which still shine bright 18 months after Rabin's assassination by a right-wing opponent of his peace moves.
Some in Netanyahu's rightist camp are also bothered by his government's scandal-prone image and feel the prime minister, the first directly elected, has ignored their concerns.
"The year ahead is the real litmus test," said a senior Likud source. "There is a great deal of bitterness in the Likud party in particular and in the right wing altogether."
Israel's political drama reaches a turning point next week when a Labour party convention is due to choose ambitious former army chief Ehud Barak as heir to Peres to lead the opposition.
After recovering from the shock of losing the election and resolving its leadership problem, Labour will give Netanyahu a fight, bolstered all the more by Barak's security credentials.

"Barak is a very formidable challenge to him, primarily because the greatest opportunity for Bibi was to be able to depict the previous Labour party government as a captive of the woolly-headed, fuzzy-thinking, sentimental left and Barak is immune to those sorts of criticisms," Heller said.
